title: 'The Moving Finger writes'
greek: Arabic/Persian qalam ('pen'), the Pen of destiny
short: Stanza LXXI (LI in 1859), FitzGerald's most quoted image of fate, drawn from Persian quatrains on the Pen that has already written all things.
body: In the first edition this was stanza LI, with 'thy Piety' and 'thy Tears'; the fifth edition prints 'your', addressing the reader more generally. Heron-Allen took Ouseley quatrain 31 as the source ('the signs of what is to be existed before; the pen never rests from good and bad ... our grieving and striving are in vain'), while Arberry named Ouseley 54 ('nothing changes from what the pen has written') the chief source; FitzGerald probably combined them. The Persian agent is the pen (qalam), not a finger: in Islamic doctrine the Pen wrote all destiny on the Preserved Tablet before creation. FitzGerald's 'Finger' draws instead on the hand that wrote on the wall in Daniel. Agatha Christie took the title of her novel The Moving Finger (1942) from this line.

title: The writing on the wall
short: A biblical reader hears Daniel 5, where 'fingers of a man's hand' write Belshazzar's doom on the palace wall during a drunken feast.
body: In Daniel 5:5 'came forth fingers of a man's hand, and wrote over against the candlestick upon the plaister of the wall of the king's palace', and the words, interpreted by Daniel, announce that Belshazzar has been weighed and found wanting (5:25-28). The parallel is apt: in both cases the writing is irrevocable and appears in the midst of wine-drinking. FitzGerald's 'Finger' is his own fusion of this biblical hand with the Persian Pen of fate (qalam), and it moves the image from scholastic theology to a sudden, almost bodily presence.

title: 'having writ'
short: 'Writ' is an archaic past participle of 'write', already old-fashioned in 1859, giving the line a scriptural weight.
body: 'Writ' was a common past tense and past participle of 'write' in earlier English (OED, write v.), as in the noun 'Holy Writ'; by the nineteenth century it was archaic. The participial phrase 'having writ' and the line-break before 'Moves on' make the grammar enact the meaning: the writing is complete before the sentence moves forward, and nothing in the next lines can reverse it. Islamic tradition has a comparable saying, that 'the pen has dried' on what has been decreed, which FitzGerald's stanza turns into an image of motion rather than stillness.

title: Enjambment: 'Moves on'
short: The verb runs over the line-break and is cut off by a colon: the line itself 'moves on' and cannot go back.
body: FitzGerald places the main verb at the start of line 2 and stops it with a colon after two syllables, so the sense of irreversible forward motion is built into the verse. The rest of the stanza is one long negative construction, 'nor all your Piety nor Wit / Shall lure it back ... / Nor all your Tears', whose repeated 'nor all' gathers the human resources only to dismiss them. The rhyme scheme is the AABA of the ruba'i (writ / Wit / it, with 'Line' unrhymed), and the final word 'it' is deliberately weak and flat, the closing of the book.

title: Piety and Wit
short: Neither religious devotion nor human intelligence can change what fate has written; the Persian sources say grieving and striving are in vain.
body: 'Wit' here means intelligence or cleverness (OED, wit n.), not humour. The pairing covers the two ways one might hope to influence destiny, prayer and reason, both dismissed. The Persian source quatrains end, in one version, with 'our grieving and striving are vain', and in another with the claim that even a lifetime of drinking bloody tears will not add a drop to what is fixed. FitzGerald's sharper opposition between piety and wit belongs to the scepticism that made the poem a Victorian manifesto against both church and intellectual system.

title: 'cancel half a Line'
short: To 'cancel' is to strike out writing; the image is a scribe's or author's correction, refused by the writer of fate.
body: 'Cancel' originally meant to cross out writing with lattice-like lines (from Latin cancelli, 'lattice'; OED, cancel v.), and in printing a 'cancel' is a substituted leaf. FitzGerald, an obsessive reviser of his own poem across four editions, chose an image from his own trade: the author may cancel his lines, but the book of fate cannot be revised. 'Lure it back' adds the idea of coaxing or bribing a reluctant creature, as if fate could be tempted by bait. 'Half a Line' is a hemistich, the half-verse unit of Persian prosody.

title: Tears that cannot wash out a word
greek: Persian khunaba ('bloody water, tears of blood')
short: Repentant tears cannot erase the ink of fate; the Persian source speaks of drinking tears of blood all one's life without changing a drop.
body: Ink could be washed from parchment, and tears of repentance are a traditional means of cleansing sin; FitzGerald denies both at once. Ouseley quatrain 54, in Arberry's account the chief source, says that even if you drink blood-tears (khunaba) all your life, not one drop will be added to what is fixed. FitzGerald drops the Persian blood and liver imagery and keeps only the tears, making the stanza cooler and more epigrammatic. The pathos of the stanza is all in that last line, and it has often been read as FitzGerald's own response to loss.

title: The Pen and the Preserved Tablet
short: Islamic tradition holds that God's Pen wrote all that would happen on the Preserved Tablet before creation; one source quatrain reads 'upon the Tablet'.
body: The Qur'an speaks of the Pen (Sura 68 is named al-Qalam) and of a 'Preserved Tablet' (al-lawh al-mahfuz, Q 85:22); theological tradition held that the Pen was the first thing created and was commanded to write all that would be until the Last Day. Heron-Allen recorded that the Calcutta manuscript version of the source quatrain reads 'upon the tablet' (bar lawh). Khayyam's quatrains, whoever wrote them, use this doctrine sceptically, as a reason why human effort and anxiety are futile; FitzGerald's 'writes' in the present tense makes the writing continuous rather than finished at the creation.
